title: Indra Asks About Deep Sleep
hook: Indra studies the self for a hundred and one years and nearly quits over deep sleep; the morning's 'I slept well' says someone was there
carry: the self is the witness, even in deep sleep
tomorrow: Kumbhakarna woke and told the king the truth. then what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the falcon folded its wings: atman rests beneath every role you play, every daytime name set down.

Indra, king of the gods, wants to know the self. In the Chandogya Upanishad he goes to Prajapati, the creator, and lives with him as a student for thirty-two years. He's taught, he leaves, he doubts, he comes back. It happens again. The third time, Prajapati points him to deep, dreamless sleep. And Indra, halfway home, stops on the road. Paraphrased: in that state a person doesn't even know, 'this is me.' It's as if he's gone to nothing. I see no good in this. Today, the king of the gods against the gap in the night.
screen: `THE KING OF THE GODS, A STUDENT.` → `THIRTY-TWO YEARS, THEN AGAIN.` → `I SEE NO GOOD IN THIS.`

segments.voice: Prajapati doesn't scold him. He says: stay five more years. Indra's whole stay comes to a hundred and one years, the text says, for one teaching. And the teaching, paraphrased: this body is mortal, held by death, but it's the dwelling of a self that is deathless and without a body. Another school asks the same question. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras count sleep among the mind's five movements: a turning that rests on absence. And the commentary credited to Vyasa notices the morning. On waking, a person says, I slept well, my mind is clear. Or, I slept badly, my mind is dull. You can't remember what never happened to you, so something was there. Here is the teaching, named plainly. Vedanta teachers call it the witness, sakshi: the self, atman, that sees waking, sees dreams, and is present even when there is nothing to see. Many teachers read the morning's 'I slept well' as the witness's fingerprint. You can't look at it, which is exactly why Indra kept missing it: it's the one doing the looking. That's why, in this teaching, you aren't your moods or your nights. Light and heavy, clear and dull, they come and go, and the witness sees them all. And as with every day in this lens: the texts describe the mind; they don't diagnose sleep. Heavy nights and dull mornings for a long stretch are a conversation for a doctor.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND ONE YEARS FOR ONE TEACHING` · `I SLEPT WELL: SOMEONE WAS THERE` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS` · `YOU AREN'T YOUR MOODS OR NIGHTS`

segments.voice: Go back to last night's sleep, not the hours but the quality, light or heavy, clear or tangled, and find one honest word for it. Then notice: something just remembered a night you were supposedly absent for. Rest a few breaths as the one who notices, not as the night. If you pray, give thanks for whatever rest there was.
Sleep. For Indra, a gap that looked like nothing; in the Yoga Sutras, a turning of the mind remembered in the morning; for Vedanta, a night the witness sees. Today's word.
Your line: the self is the witness, even in deep sleep. Indra waited a hundred and one years for it. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers read Indra's long stay with Prajapati as a lesson in how to look for the self, and point to deep sleep and the morning's 'I slept well' to teach atman as the witness, sakshi; students of the Yoga Sutras learn sleep as one of the five vrittis.

original.note: Sanskrit sakshi: witness. Vedanta's name for the self that sees waking, dream and deep sleep.

trapdoor: what you thought: in deep sleep you simply aren't there.
what it means: Indra thought so too, and Prajapati kept him five more years. 'I slept well' says something was there: the witness, atman.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 8.11's 'as if gone to destruction', Yoga Sutra 1.10's sleep resting on absence, and the commentary's argument from memory, read in Vedanta as sakshi.

chat.meaning: Indra almost gave up on deep sleep as nothing, and Prajapati taught him the deathless self; the Yoga Sutras' commentary says 'I slept well' is a memory, so sleep was experienced. Vedanta calls the one who was there sakshi, the witness: atman.

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, here a student

Prajapati.meaning: the creator, Indra's teacher in the Chandogya

Chandogya Upanishad.meaning: the Upanishad where Indra studies the self

sakshi.meaning: the witness: the self that sees

Patanjali.meaning: the teacher credited with the Yoga Sutras

Vyasa.meaning: the name traditionally given to the Yoga Sutras' first commentator

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7–8.10 (Indra and Virochana go to Prajapati; thirty-two years; the self in the water, then the dreamer; Indra doubts and returns)

Yoga Sutras 1.10 (sleep is the vritti resting on the experience of absence)
